# R2 Digest

**Source:** David Tsumura, *The Second Book of Samuel* (NICOT)

### C-R2-01
- **Claim:** Tsumura treats 2 Sam 1 as discourse-grammatical **LINK** (A/aB transitional technique) between the “Story of Saul and David” (A: 1 Sam 16–31) and the “Story of King David” (B: 2 Sam 1–20); the deaths of Saul and his heir are a step toward David’s kingship, and the narrator presents progress of events as providential act of God.
- **Quote:** “Literarily and discourse grammatically, this section (a: 2 Sam. 1) functions as a LINK between the “Story of Saul and David” (A: 1 Sam. 16–31) and the “Story of King David” (B: 2 Sam. 1–20). In other words, the present section is “a” of the A/aB pattern (“transitional technique”). … The narrator presents the whole progress of events as the providential act of God.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 10–14; section A. DEATH OF SAUL (1:1-27)
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[david]], [[saul]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R2-02
- **Claim:** Tsumura further analyzes v. 1a itself as A/aB LINK between the previous episodes (1 Sam 30 and 31) and 2 Sam 1:1-16; word order waw+David šāb (pf.) signifies simultaneity (“when David had returned”), not sequential “David returned after Saul’s death.”
- **Quote:** “verse 1a is a good example of a LINK between the previous two episodes (A: 1 Sam. 30 and 31) and the following one (B: 2 Sam. 1:1-16) in the pattern of A/aB … The word order, waw+David šāb (pf.), signifies simultaneity; hence when David had returned.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 52–57; on 1:1
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[david]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R2-03
- **Claim:** Through chronological and spatial detail (Amalekite’s ~100–112 mile run; David back two days at Ziklag after attacking Amalek), Tsumura argues the narrator makes clear David was not involved in the death of Saul and Jonathan, even though he was a Philistine vassal.
- **Quote:** “Through all these details the narrator makes it clear that David was not involved in the death of Saul and his sons, especially Jonathan, even though he was a Philistine vassal at that time.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 50–59; on 1:1–2
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[saul]], [[jonathan]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R2-04
- **Claim:** Tsumura holds the Amalekite’s account of Saul’s death **contradicts** 1 Sam 31:3-5 (self-fall on sword vs. Amalekite kills him); the easiest explanation is that the soldier lied to gain favor with David; note also 2 Sam 4:10 does not say the man had killed Saul, only that he brought the news.
- **Quote:** “This account of Saul’s death contradicts that in 1 Sam. 31:3-5. There he fell on his own sword; here the Amalekite kills him. This discrepancy is most easily explained by assuming that the soldier lied in order to gain favor with David. Note also that in 2 Sam. 4:10 David does not say that the man had killed Saul, but just that he had brought the news.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 108–109; on 1:6–10
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[saul]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R2-05
- **Claim:** Tsumura judges the Amalekite’s claim that chariots and cavalry were “closing in” on Saul on Mount Gilboa as probable **fictional embellishment**, because chariots were ineffective in mountains and Saul had retreated from Jezreel plains into Gilboa.
- **Quote:** “Saul had apparently retreated from the plains of Jezreel into the mountainous area of Gilboa to escape them, so the young man’s report that the chariots . . . were closing in on him is probably a fictional embellishment.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 112–113; on 1:6
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[saul]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R2-06
- **Claim:** On MT *baʿălê happārāšîm* (“cavalry”), Tsumura retains the longer MT against Wellhausen’s omission of *baʿălê*; *pārāš* can mean military horse or horseman, and LXX supports the MT’s longer reading.
- **Quote:** “Since this expression “is unparalleled,” Wellhausen, followed by many scholars, omits baʿălê and takes happārāšîm as “horsemen.” However, pārāš can mean either “military horse” or “horseman,” and the LXX supports the MT’s longer reading. Thus, the MT phrase baʿălê happārāšîm as it stands most likely means cavalry.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 114–115; on 1:6
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R2-07
- **Claim:** For Saul’s *kî-kol-ʿôd napšî bî* (“because all my life is still within me”), Tsumura rejects McCarter’s combined-variants reconstruction and proposes **AXB pattern** with “still” inserted between “all my life.”
- **Quote:** “However, this unusual word order might be an example of the AXB pattern, in which X (“still”) is inserted between AB (“all my life”), thus interrupting a normal sequence A-B while still modifying the phrase AB as a whole.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 120–121; on 1:9
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[saul]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R2-08

David himself had earlier refrained from killing Saul, saying he was the LORD’s anointed…”

### C-R2-09
- **Claim:** Tsumura explains 1:14–16 (David’s speech after the execution order) via **AXB**: speech of vv. 14 and 16 interrupted by v. 15; deliberate end-placement emphasizes the man’s testimony that he killed the LORD’s anointed; “Your blood be on your head” means the man, not David, is responsible for his own death.
- **Quote:** “It may be that this section follows the AXB pattern, in which David’s speech from v. 14 to v. 16 is interrupted by the insertion of v. 15. … It may be that David’s words were deliberately given at the end of the section in order to emphasize this man’s testimony that he killed the LORD’s anointed. … The expression Your blood be on your head means that “you, not I, are responsible for your own death”…”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 167–170; on 1:14–16

### C-R2-10
- **Claim:** David’s elegy (*qînāh*) expresses public and personal grief for both Saul (who sought his life) and Jonathan (who helped him); David accepts both relationships as God-given; Tsumura finds no reason to doubt Davidic authorship given the poem’s contextual unity.
- **Quote:** “David’s lament is a wonderful expression of public and personal grief. It expresses his heartfelt sorrow for the deaths of both Saul and Jonathan, for both the one who sought his life and the one who helped him with love and friendship. David accepts both of their relationships with him as God-given. … There is no reason to doubt Davidic authorship of this elegy, for the poem could hardly have been composed apart from the present context.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 174–176, 256; on 1:17–27
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[saul]], [[jonathan]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R2-11
- **Claim:** Against modern translations treating “the Bow” as a tune name, Tsumura reads *lelammēd benê-Yehûdāh qāšet* as a **heading** for how the elegy was used (possibly military training / instruction), and notes preservation in the Book of Jashar.
- **Quote:** “Most modern translations interpret the Bow as the name of the lament’s tune … but this is pure speculation. However, it may be that To teach the sons of Judah the bow … is a heading referring to how this elegy was used, like the heading of Ps. 60… This elegy was possibly used in connection with military training… This elegy (qînāh) is said to have been preserved in the Book of Jashar…”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 182–186; on 1:17–18
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R2-12
- **Claim:** Tsumura scans the elegy as a unified whole with refrain *ʾêk nāpelû gibbôrîm*; vv. 19 and 25 form inverted distant parallelism / inclusio; *haṣṣebî* “prince” = “gazelle” (Saul), later replaced by Jonathan; reverse of Jonathan–Saul (v. 22) to Saul–Jonathan (v. 23) marks change of emphasis.
- **Quote:** “How the warriors have fallen! … repeated in v. 25 and the final v. 27, is the theme that echoes throughout the elegy. Verses 19 and 25 are an inverted distant parallelism that form an “envelope” (inclusio). … The reverse of the order of the word pair from Jonathan – Saul (v. 22) to Saul – Jonathan (v. 23) indicates a change of emphasis.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 254–260; on 1:19–27
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[saul]], [[jonathan]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R2-13
- **Claim:** On 1:21a drought curse over Gilboa, Tsumura rejects traditional “fields of offerings” emendations for *śedê terûmōt*, proposing “fields of the heights” (*rwm*); scans as **AX&B** broken-up bicolon; parallels Ugaritic Aqhat drought curse (*bl ṭl bl rbb*), which Gordon links to the tradition that slaying a hero brings drought.
- **Quote:** “Instead of emending the text… I would suggest “heights,” based on the verbal root *rwm… It is more likely that śedê terûmōt “fields of heights”… is parallel to mountains of Gilboa… AX&B pattern… The expression no dew and no rain is virtually the same as the Ugaritic curse formula bl ṭl bl rbb… C. H. Gordon notes that it fits in with “the widespread idea that the slaying of a hero brings drought and famine…”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 270–316; on 1:21
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[saul]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R2-14
- **Claim:** Tsumura stresses that “not anointed with oil” in 1:21 refers to Saul’s **shield** (leather treatment), not to Saul himself, whom David repeatedly calls anointed; “was defiled” // “was not anointed with oil” is A, not B (word + negated antonym) in chiasmus.
- **Quote:** “The phrase not anointed does not refer to Saul, whom David repeatedly refers to as “anointed” (v. 16; also 1 Sam. 24:6, etc.). … The two expressions, was defiled and was not anointed with oil, constitute the A, not B pattern…”

### C-R2-17
- **Claim:** After Saul’s death David inquires of the LORD in **two steps** and is directed to Hebron; Tsumura notes Hebron’s Abrahamic/Calebite/priestly associations and strategic-political advantages for uniting southern clans, while stressing David’s willingness to be led by the Lord’s word.
- **Quote:** “As in 23:2-4 and 10-12, David inquires of the Lord in two steps to make it certain that the Lord himself was guiding him… But even though he may have already given thought to the matter, David inquires, “Where shall I go up to?” Perhaps this indicates his willingness to be led by the Lord’s word.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 409–441; on 2:1–3
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R2-18
- **Claim:** Men of Judah anoint David king over the **house of Judah**—first occurrence of that phrase in the Bible; this is first step actualizing monarchy after Samuel’s anointing over “Israel”; no prophet mentioned; Tsumura links *bêt dāwīd* to the late-ninth-century Tell Dan inscription as earliest extrabiblical attestation of the name David.
- **Quote:** “David is here officially anointed as a king over the house of Judah. In 1 Sam. 16:1, 13 he was anointed by Samuel to become the future king over “Israel”… This is the first occurrence of the phrase the house of Judah in the Bible. Compare “the house of David” (bêt dāwīd) … as well as in the late-ninth-century Tell Dan inscription … the earliest attested extrabiblical document that mentions the name David.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 445–451; on 2:4a
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R2-19
- **Claim:** David’s message to Jabesh-gilead (loyal burial of Saul) is not purely political: *ḥesed weʾĕmet* blessing and *ʿāśāh ṭôbāh* may imply treaty/friendship, yet Tsumura stresses religious tone; David presents himself as successor and invites them, but they apparently do not accept (Gilead under Ishbosheth, v. 9).
- **Quote:** “However, one gets the impression that David was not simply motivated by politics when he sent messengers to Jabesh-gilead. … while such a political aspect certainly existed … David’s word has a religious tone, centering more on the gracious and truthful deed of the Lord… But apparently they do not accept it, as Gilead becomes part of Ishbosheth’s kingdom (v. 9).”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 482–496; on 2:4b–7

### C-R2-20
- **Claim:** Abner installs **Ishbosheth** (Chronicles “Ishbaal”) at Mahanaim as king over northern/Transjordan and central Israel; Tsumura treats *bosheth* as euphemistic substitution for *baal*, but argues Saul would not name sons after foreign Baal—so “lord” may refer to Yahweh; capital in Transjordan signals precariousness; from 2:8–11 and 3:6–11 Ishbosheth appears little more than Abner’s puppet.
- **Quote:** “Ishbosheth appears as “Ishbaal” in the genealogies in 1 Chr. 8:33, 9:39. Since Ishbosheth probably means “Man-of-shame,” the bosheth in Samuel is usually taken as … “a euphemistic substitution” for “baal”… Certainly, there is no reason why Saul should name his sons after the foreign god Baal… Therefore, it is often suggested that the “lord” in these names refers to the Lord, i.e., “Yahweh.” … The fact that the capital had to be in Transjordan suggests the precariousness of Ishbosheth’s rule. … it appears that Ishbosheth was little more than his puppet.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 509–525; on 2:8–11
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[abner]], [[saul]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

- **Quote:** “David apparently has decided that his allegiance to Saul as God’s anointed king does not extend to Saul’s descendants… in 2 Sam. 4:11 he just refers to Ishbosheth as a “righteous man,” not as a king or an anointed one as he had referred to Saul… Thus, for a time, there were two kings in the land of Israel. ### C-R2-22
- **Claim:** Hostilities open at Gibeon (pool identified with Pritchard’s Great Pool); Tsumura suggests David may have been negotiating with Gibeonites (deep resentment against Saul, 2 Sam 21) as with Jabesh; Abner proposes a *neʿārîm* contest—Tsumura doubts Abner and Joab could decide kingship by such a contest alone (contra McCarter/Fensham divine-will reading).
- **Quote:** “It is not unlikely that David was negotiating with the Gibeonites as he had attempted to do with Jabesh-gilead, since they harbored a deep resentment against Saul (2 Sam. 21:1-9). … While such contests might be a way of deciding the divine will about some things, it seems unlikely that Abner and Joab could decide the matter of the kingship on their own.”

### C-R2-24
- **Claim:** Chapter 3’s concern is to show David not guilty of Abner’s (or later Ishbosheth’s) death—the most “apologetic” tone in the Story of King David; yet from the larger narrative, motivating force is Yahweh’s will and special favor for David, enacted through interplay of Ishbosheth, David, Abner, and Joab (McCarter cited).
- **Quote:** “Clearly, one of the concerns of the author is to show that David was not guilty of involvement in the deaths of Abner or Ishbosheth. In fact, the present section is the most “apologetic” in tone of the “Story of King David.” However, as McCarter notes, “From the perspective of the larger narrative, the motivating force was Yahweh’s will and his special favor for David.” But this event took place by the “interplay of four human personalities,” Ishbosheth, David, Abner, and Joab.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 683–687; on 3:1–39 intro

### C-R2-26
- **Claim:** Ishbosheth’s accusation that Abner went in to Rizpah (Saul’s concubine) angers Abner; taking king’s wives could signal throne claim, but Tsumura notes it was a single concubine, so even if true it need not mean Abner claimed kingship; Abner then vows to transfer kingdom to David “as the LORD swore to David” (implied in 1 Sam 15:28; 16:13)—Tsumura rejects need for prophetic/Deuteronomistic interpolation.
- **Quote:** “Taking the king’s wives seems to have been considered a prerogative of the throne… So, even if the accusation was true, it does not necessarily mean that Abner was trying to claim the kingship. … This promise of the Lord is implied in 1 Sam. 15:28 and 16:13… One need not assume here a prophetic or a later Deuteronomistic interpolation as some scholars often assume.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 742–781; on 3:7–11
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[abner]], [[david]], [[saul]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R2-27
- **Claim:** Abner offers covenant to turn all Israel to David; David’s condition is return of **Michal** (still legally his wife—bridal price paid, no divorce); Ishbosheth’s involvement surprisingly recognizes David’s connection to Saul’s house; not a violation of Deut 24:1–4; request may be both political and personal.
- **Quote:** “David had legally paid the bridal price and never divorced Michal even though she remarried, so she is still legally his wife. … Ishbosheth’s involvement would mean that even he recognized David’s connection with the house of Saul. … Note that this is not violating the law in Deut. 24:1-4, for David did not divorce Michal. … David’s request for Michal may have been in part political, but since he had Abner’s support even without that, it may also have been personal.”

### C-R2-28
- **Claim:** Abner rallies elders of Israel and Benjaminites with an oracle that by David’s hand the LORD will save Israel from Philistines; *ṭôb* (“good”) has treaty meaning; thrice-repeated “went in peace” (3:21–23) emphasizes David’s innocence; Joab murders Abner as blood-avenger for Asahel, but David (and 1 K 2:5) deny that duty properly applies to battlefield killing in time of peace.

### C-R2-29
- **Claim:** Joab’s motives mix concern for David’s position, his own position, and private vengeance; David times meeting to avoid Joab; David publicly declares innocence, curses Joab’s house, stages detailed funeral and elegy (only funeral described in detail in OT); people and all Israel know Abner’s death was not the king’s will; David still “weak” vs. “too wild” sons of Zeruiah—cannot yet punish Joab.
- **Quote:** “Here, as later in 18:14 and 20:10, the motive for Joab’s actions can be seen as concern for David’s position (v. 25), concern for his own position … private vengeance (v. 30), or a mixture. … Joab is apparently too important and useful for David to punish, so he does the best he can by cursing him and having a splendid funeral for Abner… This is the only funeral described in detail in the Old Testament. … And all the people and all Israel knew that day that it was not the king’s will that Abner son of Ner be put to death.”

### C-R2-32
- **Claim:** Against widespread LXX preference for 4:6, Tsumura defends **MT originality** via discourse structure (SETTING / EVENT / PROCEDURE “as takers of wheat” / TERMINUS): brothers pretended to be wheat purchasers to enter; v. 7 expands v. 6 rather than being later rephrasing; rejects Mastéy’s “grain robbers already inside” double-strike reading.
- **Quote:** “Many emendations of the text have been suggested, but a close look at the sequence of the verbal forms suggests that most of them are unnecessary. … The parenthetical sentence … as takers of wheat (v. 6a), is a procedural discourse (“how”) … This suggests that they pretended to be purchasers of wheat in order to gain entry into the house. … Some claim that v. 7 is a later rephrasing of the account of v. 6.
